courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Intro to Philosophy-ACP
courses.description: Consideration of some main problems of philosophy concerning, for example, knowledge, God, mind and body, and human freedom. Course is identical to PHIL 101 except for the additional writing component. Credit is not given for both PHIL 100 and PHIL 101.
courses.prereqText: Completion of campus Composition I general education requirement.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy
courses.description: [IAI Code: H4900] Consideration of some main problems of philosophy concerning, for example, knowledge, God, mind and body, and human freedom. Credit is not given toward graduation for: Credit is not given for both PHIL 101 and PHIL 100.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Logic and Reasoning
courses.description: Practical study of logical reasoning; techniques for analyzing and criticizing arguments, with emphasis on assessing the logical coherence of what we read and write.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Logic and Reasoning QR II
courses.description: Practical study of logical reasoning; techniques for analyzing and criticizing arguments, with emphasis on assessing the logical coherence of what we read and write. Credit is not given for both PHIL 103 and PHIL 102.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Intro to Ethics-ACP
courses.description: Some basic questions of ethics, discussed in the light of influential ethical theories and with reference to specific moral problems, such as: What makes an action morally right? Are moral standards absolute or relative? What is relation between personal morality and social morality, and between social morality and law? Course is identical to PHIL 105 except for the additional writing component. Credit is not given for both PHIL 104 and either PHIL 105 or PHIL 106.
courses.prereqText: Completion of campus Composition I general education requirement.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Ethics
courses.description: Some basic questions of ethics, discussed in the light of influential ethical theories and with reference to specific moral problems, such as: what makes an action morally right? are moral standards absolute or relative? what is the relation between personal morality and social morality, and between social morality and law? Credit is not given for both PHIL 105 and either PHIL 104 or PHIL 106.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics and Social Policy
courses.description: Examination of the moral aspects of social problems, and a survey of ethical principles formulated to validate social policy. Credit is not given for both PHIL 106 and either PHIL 104 or PHIL 105.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Intro to Political Philosophy
courses.description: Introduction to core ideas in political and legal philosophy, for example, rights, equality, political obligations, legitimacy of states, nationalism, and oppression.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Religion & Society in West I
courses.description: Introduction to classic writers and texts in Western religious and social thought from antiquity to the Enlightenment, with emphasis on their social and historical contexts. Same as JS 108, ANTH 108, and PHIL 108.
courses.pointerText: Same as ANTH 108, JS 108, and REL 108. See REL 108.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Religion & Society in West II
courses.description: Introduction to classic writers and texts in Western religious and social thought from the Enlightenment to the present, with emphasis on their social and historical contexts. Same as ANTH 109 and PHIL 109..
courses.pointerText: Same as ANTH 109 and REL 109. See REL 109.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: World Religions
courses.description: [IAI Code: H5904N] Survey of the leading living religions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam; examination of basic texts and of philosophic theological elaborations of each religion. Same as PHIL 110.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Living Well Online
courses.description: Philosophical reflection on human happiness, flourishing, and virtue, with a focus on the challenge of living well in a digital age. Along with classic philosophical texts by Plato, Aristotle, and others, we will read and discuss a number of contemporary authors who have reflected on the ways that our lives are changed by the pervasive presence of digital technology.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: The Meaning of Life
courses.description: What is the meaning of life? Does life even have a meaning? If life doesn’t have a meaning, is that a problem? This course examines these and related questions, and critically surveys answers from a variety of religious, philosophical, literary, and scientific sources. While this course won’t try to tell you what the meaning of your life really is or should be, it will give you tools to help you reach your own conclusions.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Undergraduate Open Seminar
courses.description: Undergraduate seminar with variable topics in the area of philosophy. Approved for both Letter and S/U grading. May be repeated in the same term up to 6 UG hours if topics vary or in separate terms up to 6 UG hours if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy in Literature
courses.description: Consideration of the philosophical themes implicit in a variety of important literary works, both classical and modern; may include such authors as Sophocles, Shakespeare, Goethe, Dostoevsky, and Sartre.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Symbolic Logic
courses.description: Introduction to the techniques of formal logic, dealing primarily with truth-functional logic and quantification theory.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ancient Philosophy
courses.description: [IAI Code: H4901] Introduction to ancient philosophy, concentrating on Plato and Aristotle, dealing with such topics as metaphysics, ethics, and the theory of knowledge. Same as CLCV 203.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Early Modern Philosophy
courses.description: [IAI Code: H4902] The history of philosophy from Descartes to Kant, concentrating on such topics as metaphysics, ethics, and the theory of knowledge.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Asian Philosophy
courses.description: Investigation of some of the most influential philosophical movements and texts of India and China: the Vedas, Upanishads, Buddhism, Confucianism, Mohism, Daoism, and other texts and movements. Of particular focus is how these traditions answer philosophical questions such as what is the good life? How should society be structured? What is knowledge? Is all knowledge relative? What is the nature of reality? What is the individual’s relationship to society or the environment?.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics
courses.description: [IAI Code: H4904] Problems in ethical theory; the nature of right and wrong, justice, conscience, moral feelings, etc.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Biomedical Ethics
courses.description: Philosophical study of selected moral and social problems concerning medicine and biology, such as euthanasia, abortion, allocation of scarce medical resources, health care and rights, and genetic engineering.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Class, Gender, and Race
courses.description: Introduction to philosophical discussion of class, gender, and race. Conversations will span class consciousness, contemporary unionizing, concepts of gender, orientation, defining race, and experiences of racial ambiguity. The course integrates reflections on intersectionality throughout to explore the congruence and dissimilarity of discourses on class, gender, and race.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophical Foundations of Computer Science
courses.description: Introduction to certain ideas and issues at the intersection of computer science and philosophy. Students will focus on foundational questions related to the birth of computer science as a discipline, philosophical issues regarding knowledge and reality that researchers face in the frontiers of contemporary computer science, and current ethical issues related to the uses of machines and computers in society.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Minds & Machines
courses.description: Introduction to certain ideas and issues at the intersection of computer science and philosophy. Students will focus on the nature of human minds and brains in light of what we know about machine “minds” and “hardware” (and vice versa), as well as on philosophical considerations of the societal effects and implications of the rise of intelligent machines.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Religion Intro
courses.description: [IAI Code: H4905] Introduction to philosophical analysis of religious thought and experience. Same as REL 230.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Happiness and the Good Life
courses.description: Explores the foundational question of what it means to live well or to live a good, meaningful, and happy life. This course introduces students to resources and concepts from Western philosophical and theological traditions to explore this central question. Students will critically and charitably engage these traditions, determining what resources they might offer and what considerations they might neglect. Same as PHIL 231.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Conceptions of Human Nature
courses.description: Comparative examination of important historical and contemporary conceptions of human nature.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Science
courses.description: Investigation of the nature of scientific knowledge by examining archetypal examples from physical science (e.g., Ptolemaic and Copernican astronomy); nature of scientific truth, validation of theories, nature of scientific theories, evolution of theories, experimental procedure, role of presuppositions, scientific revolutions, etc.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Elmnts Semantics & Pragmatics
courses.description: Introduction to the theory of meaning for natural language, including techniques for the description of lexical meaning, compositional determination of phrase and sentence meaning, and pragmatic effects on interpretation in context. Same as PHIL 307.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics and Engineering
courses.description: Ethical issues in the practice of engineering: safety and liability, professional responsibility to clients and employers, whistle-blowing, codes of ethics, career choice, and legal obligations. Philosophical analysis of normative ethical theories. Case studies. Same as PHIL 316. Credit is not given for both ECE 316 and either CS 210 or CS 211. Junior standing is required.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Thinking and Reasoning
courses.description: An overview of historical and contemporary research on thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving. Topics will include normative systems of logic, defeasible/non-monotonic reasoning, psychological models of reasoning, heuristic problem-solving, insight and creativity, Bayesian decision-making, decision-making biases, and fast-and-frugal heuristics.
courses.prereqText: Either PSYC 100 and PSYC 224, or PHIL 101 and PHIL 102, or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Non-Classical Logics
courses.description: Exploration of a range of formal alternatives to and extensions of classical (deductive) logic, such as modal logic, intuitionist logic, and relevant logic. Elements of syntax and semantics for each logic, along with a tableau proof theory, will be discussed. Students will also engage with the philosophical motivations behind these logics and critically examine the challenges they present.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Current Controversies
courses.description: Philosophical examination of positions taken on some issue of current concern, for example, human sexuality, death and dying, feminism, race, intelligence, war, sociobiology, and environmental ethics. See Class Schedule for current topics. May be repeated with approval.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Individual Study
courses.description: Readings in selected philosophical topics. Course may be taken by honors students in partial fulfillment of department honors requirements. May be repeated to a maximum of 6 hours in separate terms.
courses.prereqText: Open to juniors and seniors with a grade-point average of 3.0 only by prior arrangement with a member of the faculty and with consent of the department director of undergraduate studies or the chair.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Medieval Philosophy
courses.description: History of philosophy from St. Augustine to William of Ockham. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Logic and Linguistic Analysis
courses.description: Introduction to the theory of logic as applied in linguistic analysis. Same as PHIL 407. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.
courses.prereqText: For undergraduate students: LING 307 or equivalent background with consent of instructor.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Classical Ancient Philosophers
courses.description: Intensive study of one ancient philosopher or the intensive study of a major philosophical problem through the consideration of a number of ancient philosophers; chief emphasis on Plato and/or Aristotle. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours. May be repeated with approval, if topics vary.
courses.prereqText: One course in philosophy, preferably PHIL 203.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Nineteenth Century Philosophy
courses.description: Examination of the thought of such major figures as Hegel, Marx, and Nietzsche. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. May be repeated in the same or separate semesters up to 6 undergraduate hours or up to 8 graduate hours with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Classical Modern Philosophers
courses.description: Intensive study of one classical modern philosopher or the intensive study of major philosophical problem through the consideration of a number of classical modern philosophers, e.g., Descartes, Leibniz, Locke, Hume, Kant, and Hegel. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours. May be repeated with approval, if topics vary.
courses.prereqText: One course in philosophy, preferably PHIL 206.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Major Recent Philosophers
courses.description: Intensive study of one or two important philosophers of the present century, e.g., Wittgenstein, Dewey, Heidegger, or Quine. Topics vary; see Class Schedule. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours. May be repeated with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Space, Time, and Matter-ACP
courses.description: Identical to PHYS 420 except for the additional writing component including a final term paper. Same as PHIL 419. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. Credit is not given for both PHYS 419 and PHYS 420.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Space, Time, and Matter
courses.description: Philosophical examination of some fundamental concepts and theories of the physical world, such as time, matter, space, and geometry; interpretation of quantum theory. Same as PHIL 420. 2 undergraduate hours. 2 graduate hours. Credit is not given for both PHYS 420 and PHYS 419.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethical Theories
courses.description: Systematic study of selected classics in moral philosophy by such philosophers as Aristotle, Hume, Mill, Kant, and Nietzsche. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Recent Developments in Ethics
courses.description: Intensive treatment of issues in contemporary ethical theory. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. May be repeated in the same or separate semesters up to 6 undergraduate hours or up to 8 graduate hours with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Religion
courses.description: Considers central issues in the philosophy of religion, e.g., the justification of religious belief, the nature of God, religious experience, etc. Same as REL 424. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Mind
courses.description: Philosophical problems arising in connection with mental phenomena; the relation of mind and body; free will and determinism; our knowledge of other minds; and the self and personal identity. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Metaphysics
courses.description: Investigation of various metaphysical issues concerning, for example, existence, particulars and universals, causation, laws of nature, time, personal identity, material objects, and modality. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Value Theory
courses.description: Study of the nature and status of values, and of variable topics in value theory, e.g., different types of values, and problems of truth, justifiability, objectivity and relativism with respect to them. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. May be repeated in the same or separate terms up to 6 undergraduate hours or up to 8 graduate hours with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Theory of Knowledge
courses.description: Investigation of issues concerning, for example, the nature and possibility of knowledge; its forms and limits; its relation to belief, truth, and justification; and the nature of truth. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Evolutionary Neuroscience
courses.description: Current methods, tools, and progress in evolutionary biology and quantitative genetics of brain and behavior of vertebrates. Same as IB 436, NEUR 433, and PHIL 433. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.
courses.pointerText: Same as IB 436, NEUR 433 and PSYC 433. See PSYC 433.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Social Philosophy
courses.description: Selected topics from the nature of social organization, nature and convention, utility, justice, equality, liberty, rights, and duties. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. May be repeated in the same or separate semesters up to 6 undergraduate hours or up to 8 graduate hours with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Phil of Law and of the State
courses.description: Examination of issues in the philosophy of law, such as the nature of law, law and morality, justice, liberty and authority, punishment, and legal responsibility. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. May be repeated in the same or separate semesters up to 6 undergraduate hours or up to 8 graduate hours with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Language
courses.description: Historical or comparative study of the philosophy of language. Same as LING 438. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Mathematics
courses.description: Introduction to some of the main philosophical problems and contemporary viewpoints concerning mathematical concepts, mathematical methods, and the nature of mathematical truth. Same as MATH 439. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: Provides students with an understanding of ethical challenges presented by the development of AI. Topics may include the role of AI in education and ethical theory, the ethical implications of data collection and surveillance, the future of work, bias in algorithms, the moral status of AI systems, and existential risk. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.
courses.prereqText: One course in philosophy or sophomore standing.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Existential Philosophy
courses.description: Study of a selection of the major writings of the more important existential philosophers, e.g., Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and de Beauvoir. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: The AI Revolution
courses.description: We are in the midst of what many have called an “Artificial Intelligence (AI) Revolution.” This revolution is comparable in scope and impact to other major transformations in human history, such as the industrial revolution. The purpose of this course is to help students understand how and why recent developments in AI have begun to challenge traditional ways of thinking, while presenting novel and pressing ethical, social, interpretive, conceptual, technological, and existential questions. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Phenomenology
courses.description: Study of the development of phenomenology from Husserl to the present. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Formal Logic and Philosophy
courses.description: Techniques and results of symbolic logic, with special attention to topics of philosophical importance. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Advanced Symbolic Logic
courses.description: Completeness, compactness, and Lowenheim-Skolem theorems for first-order logic; incompleteness and undecidability of formal systems; and additional material on proof theory, model theory, or axiomatic set theory as time permits. 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Advances in Brain and Cognitive Science
courses.description: An in-depth, integrative overview of the major themes in the study of Cognitive Science, including cognition as computation, the relation between mind and brain, computability and the role of heuristics in "solving" unsolvable problems, and the logical/mathematical foundations of these themes. Specific topics covered include inverse optics and vision; induction and reasoning; learnability and language; philosophy of minds and brains; evolution; artificial intelligence and computational modeling; information theory; knowledge representation. The emphasis throughout is on the interrelations among these topics as examples of important but fundamentally unsolvable problems. Same as PHIL 458. 3 undergraduate hours. No graduate credit.
courses.prereqText: One of PSYC 224, PSYC 248, PHIL 202, PHIL 270, or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Statistics
courses.description: Introduction to philosophical issues related to statistics. Topics include the interpretation of probability, the difference between description and inference, the notion of evidential support, the relationship between statistics and inductive logic, the use and abuse of mathematical models, the nature of randomness and chance, the role of values in statistical modeling and decision, and the ethical practice of statistics. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.
courses.prereqText: At least one course in philosophy, and at least one course in statistics. Restricted to Junior, Senior or Graduate standing.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Contemporary Phil of Science
courses.description: Examines important developments and controversies in recent philosophy of science. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours. May be repeated in the same or separate semesters up to 6 undergraduate hours or up to 8 graduate hours with approval, if topics vary.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Kierkegaard and the Self
courses.description: Soren Kierkegaard is an early author who wrestled with the concept of the individual self and championed subjective experience as a counterbalance to objective rationalism. Students in this seminar-style course will gain extensive familiarity with Kierkegaard's major works, as well as how they relate to two currents in 19th century society, existentialism and pietism. These works will be evaluated within their particular Nordic literary context, through critical analysis of related novels, plays and films by Andersen, Ibsen, Bremer, Strindberg, Lagerlof, Blixen, and Bergman (readings in English translation). Same as CWL 472, PHIL 472, and REL 472. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.
courses.pointerText: Same as CWL 472, REL 472, and SCAN 472. See SCAN 472.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Philosophy of Psychology
courses.description: Psychology, broadly construed, is a cluster of disciplines devoted to the study of mind and behavior, including cognitive and developmental psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Investigates the relationships that these disciplines bear to one another and of their overall potential to resolve age-old philosophical questions about the mind. Same as PSYC 477. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.
courses.prereqText: Two courses in philosophy or two courses in psychology or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Thesis
courses.description: Special training in philosophical investigation. Course may be taken by students pursuing graduation with distinction in partial fulfillment of those requirements. 2 to 4 undergraduate hours. No graduate credit. May be repeated to a maximum of 4 undergraduate hours.
courses.prereqText: Open to seniors with a grade-point average of 3.5 in all philosophy courses only by prior arrangement with a member of the faculty and with consent of the department director of undergraduate studies or the chair.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Capstone Seminar
courses.description: Capstone course required for all philosophy majors. Students will explore in depth a specific topic either in the history of philosophy or in contemporary practical or theoretical philosophy and will write a substantial original essay appropriate for a senior thesis. Topics will differ by section and semester. 3 undergraduate hours. No graduate credit.
courses.prereqText: PHIL 202, PHIL 203, PHIL 206, PHIL 222, PHIL 223. Restricted to Philosophy and CS + Philosophy majors with Senior Standing. Philosophy majors (and CS + Philosophy majors matriculated before Fall 2020) are required to have PHIL 202 (or equivalent), PHIL 203, and PHIL 206. CS + Philosophy majors (matriculated after Fall 2020) are required to have PHIL 202 (or equivalent), PHIL 222, and PHIL 223.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar on the History of Philosophy
courses.description: Study of selected major philosophers, movements, problems, or topics in the history of philosophy. Approved for Letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Formal Semantics I
courses.description: Introduction to formal semantic theory for natural language, with attention to quantification, anaphora, tense, intensionality, and related topics. Same as PHIL 507.
courses.prereqText: LING 407 or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Ethical Theory
courses.description: Intensive study of problems in ethical theory. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Social Philosophy
courses.description: Seminar designed to study special problems in social philosophy. See Schedule for current topics. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Philosophy of Logic
courses.description: Selected topics in contemporary logical theory. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar in Cognitive Science
courses.description: In-depth view of cognitive science: the study of mind and intelligence. Covers major areas of cognitive science including: anthropology, artificial intelligence, cognitive neuroscience, cognitive psychology, emotions, linguistics, and philosophy. Lectures focus on prominent questions and issues in each area highlighted by descriptions of current research. Also explores interconnections among these fields. Same as ANTH 514, CS 549, EPSY 551, LING 570, and PHIL 514.
courses.prereqText: Minimally second semester graduate standing in a cognitive science discipline including: anthropology, computer science, educational psychology, electrical engineering, linguistics, philosophy, psychology, or consent of instructor.
courses.pointerText: Same as PSYC 514, ANTH 514, CS 549, EPSY 551, and LING 570. See PSYC 514.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Philosophy of Science
courses.description: Various problems arising from specific studies in philosophy pertaining to science and vice versa. To be offered with varying topics. Course Information:Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Contemporary Problems
courses.description: Intensive study of selected problems or topics in contemporary philosophy. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Theory of Knowledge
courses.description: Selected topics and writings of major importance in the contemporary philosophy of knowledge. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Letter grading applies when offered for 4 hours of credit. For Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students this course is approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours of credit.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Seminar Philosophy of Mind
courses.description: Selected topics from major writings in the philosophy of mind. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated in the same or separate terms. Approved for letter grading when offered for 4 hours; approved for S/U grading when offered for 2 hours - only available for Stage 3 Philosophy PhD students.
courses.prereqText: Consent of instructor for non-philosophy graduate students.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Dissertation Seminar
courses.description: Ongoing dissertation seminar required for all students who have passed the prelim requirement. Approved for S/U grading only. May be repeated in separate terms to a maximum of 24 hours.
courses.prereqText: Restricted to students satisfying requirements for the Ph.D. degree.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Formal Semantics II
courses.description: A continuation of LING 507 covering advanced topics in formal semantic theory. Same as PHIL 547.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Pragmatics
courses.description: Examination of the major theoretical frameworks in Gricean and post-Gricean pragmatics with an emphasis on theories of implicature, speech acts and im/politeness. Same as PHIL 551.
courses.prereqText: LING 501 and LING 507, or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Individual Topics
courses.description: Individual study and oral and written reports on topics not covered in other courses. Topics and plan of study must be approved by the candidate's adviser and by the staff member who directs the work. May be repeated. (Summer session, 2 to 8 hours).

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Directed Research
courses.description: Restricted to students satisfying requirements for the master's degree by writing a substantial essay. Approved for letter and S/U grading. May be repeated. Normally taken for 8 hours credit but may be taken for 12 hours credit with consent of department chair.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Thesis Research
courses.description: Approved for S/U grading only. May be repeated in the same term or in separate terms.
